title: Etch A Sketch!
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant discuss the Etch A Sketch toy: its French origins with inventor Andre Cassan, who got the idea from metal dust shavings on a decal at the Lincrusta wall-covering factory near Paris, the patent filed under accountant Arthur Grangenny, the sale to Ohio Art, its 1960 launch with TV commercials, its pop-culture moments, the later sale to Spin Master, and tips on making Etch A Sketch art. The episode opens with a list of classic toys covered on the show and ends with a listener mail segment about Jerry's miso soup eating.

segments.title: Opening and list of classic toys
segments.summary: The hosts run through a list of classic toys the show has covered, including Slinky, Lego, Barbie, G.I. Joe, Hot Wheels, Easy-Bake Oven, Play-Doh, Silly Putty, boomerangs, Monopoly, Yo-Yos, Hula Hoops, and Teddy Ruxpin, and tease Etch A Sketch as a top-100 toy of the century.

segments.title: French origins and Andre Cassan's invention
segments.summary: Etch A Sketch originated in France. Around 1954 or 1956 in Vitry-sur-Seine, Andre Cassan worked at Lincrusta, a metal wall-covering maker, where metal dust on a decal led him to the idea of a drawing toy.

segments.title: Patent and how Etch A Sketch works
segments.summary: Cassan partnered with Paul Chase, whose plastic injection molding company provided funding. Accountant Arthur Grangenny filed the 1959 US patent in his name. The hosts explain the aluminum powder screen, the stylus moved by knobs through pulleys and gears, and how shaking erases the drawing.

segments.title: Pitch to Ohio Art and licensing deal
segments.summary: Cassan tried to sell the idea at the 1959 Nuremberg Toy Fair for a high price and was turned down by toymakers including Ohio Art. Ohio Art later bought the US license for about fifteen or twenty-five thousand dollars. Chief engineer Jerry Burger replaced the joystick with knobs. Ohio Art's history with metal lithography is covered.

segments.title: 1960 launch and television commercials
segments.summary: Ohio Art rebranded the toy as Etch A Sketch and launched it for the 1960 holiday season, selling about 600,000 units at $2.09. Its TV commercial with animation helped popularity, and the company reportedly manufactured until Christmas Eve to meet demand.

segments.title: Pop culture, sales spikes, and later ownership
segments.summary: Sales rose after pop-culture moments, including Republican and Democrat-branded versions and Toy Story's character. Ohio Art later struggled, moved manufacturing to China around 2001, and sold the Etch A Sketch brand to Spin Master.
topics: Republican and Democrat Etch A Sketch

segments.title: Etch A Sketch variations, app, and art
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Doodle Sketch, the Plug 'n Play TV version, the mobile app that etchifies photos, and the Sketch Animator. They cover Etch A Sketch artists such as George Vlosits III, Jane Labowitch, and Ryan Burton, and techniques like single-line retracing. They also mention preserving artwork by drilling out the powder.

segments.title: Listener mail about Jerry's miso soup
segments.summary: A listener named Kim Cooper writes asking about Jerry's miso soup eating during recordings, and the hosts discuss miso paste.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give the contact email and website and sign off.
